stories.topic: The heart attack he never noticed
stories.summary: After digging through dusty old letters for the 'Objects From Our Past' episode and attending a conference in early December, Amit fell ill with something COVID-like. Then came what he took for food poisoning: acidity, bad bouts of vomiting at night, and a tightening in the chest whenever he exerted himself. He assumed it was a lingering lung or viral issue. Lancelot Pinto found his lungs performing at 103–106% of normal for his age and sent him to a cardiologist. An HS troponin test showed he had already had a minor heart attack without noticing. A CT scan found an 80–90% block in the right coronary artery, and by the time of the angioplasty it was 100%. A stent requires lifelong aspirin and he was allergic to it, so he first spent a day or two in ICU being 'desensitized' to aspirin, and then got a drug-eluting stent. Because the procedure carried a 1–2% mortality risk, he wrote 'if I die' emails, briefed Gaurav Chintamani on the two Seen and the Unseen episodes in the bank, and got the next EIE episode ready for Nomsita to publish.
stories.insight: Our picture of catastrophe comes from cinema, but real danger often arrives without a soundtrack. The faint, persistent signals are the warning. The trap is explaining them away with the most convenient story: dust, COVID, bad food.
stories.quote: The way I imagine a heart attack is that there's a dramatic moment, background music increases. And Yeah, and then you clutch your heart and all kinds of things happening. There was nothing dramatic.

stories.topic: Venomous snake bites are not cinematic
stories.summary: Ajay offers an analogy for the silent heart attack. As a city child he imagined a cobra bite as a cataclysm: fangs gripping your calf, and you drop dead moments later. In reality venomous snakes do a high-speed bite, pump in venom like a hypodermic syringe and get away immediately, so the victim feels very little. You may only see two puncture marks, and the drama unfolds over minutes and hours. With common krait bites, people are bitten in their sleep, never wake up, and are found dead in the morning.
stories.insight: The deadliest events can feel like nothing at the moment they happen. Calibrating your alarm to drama rather than to consequences is how you get killed.
stories.quote: What they do is they do a high speed bite, the fangs get into your body, they pump venom into your body, they disengage immediately and get far away from you because why do they want to get into trouble?

stories.topic: His father's heart attack, forty years earlier
stories.summary: When Sudhir Sarnobat called during Amit's procedure, Ajay was at peak anxiety, because heart attacks are personal for him. In 1982 his father had a small heart attack that was only recognised as one a month later. None of today's tools existed; he was prescribed nitroglycerin as a blood thinner. In 1984 he had a second heart attack and died, aged 58.
stories.insight: Almost the same event, four decades apart, ended in death in 1984 and in a one-hour procedure in 2025. That gap is what the 'miracles of modern science' actually mean in a single family's life.
stories.quote: He was prescribed nitroglycerin as a blood thinner and in nineteen eighty four he had a second heart attack and he died and he was all of fifty eight.

stories.topic: Werner Forssmann puts a catheter into his own heart (1929)
stories.summary: In 1929 Berlin, catheters existed and early angiography of other organs had begun, but the dogma said never go near the heart. Werner Forssmann, a 25-year-old doctor, believed a catheter could safely reach it, and his superior forbade the experiment. His devoted nurse refused to let someone so important risk himself and insisted he experiment on her. He strapped her down and gave her local anaesthetic. Then, while she waited, he inserted the catheter into his own arm and guided it up using a mirror. He walked to the X-ray lab and, with a fluoroscope, guided it into his right atrium. He repeated it nine more times on himself and lost his job. His next boss, Ferdinand Sauerbruch, sneered at such circus experiments, and by 1932 Forssmann had left for urology. He joined the Nazi party and spent five years imprisoned after the war, but his work was rediscovered and he won a Nobel Prize in the 1950s. He died in 1979, at 75, of a heart attack. Narendra Shenoy told Amit this story while he was in hospital.
stories.insight: A procedure that is routine in 2025 began with one rebel betting his own body against the consensus. Amit separates art from artist: Forssmann's Nazi membership doesn't erase what he contributed.
stories.quote: He says, I will not put something in someone else's heart, I'll put it in my own heart.

stories.topic: Barry Marshall swallows the ulcer bacterium
stories.summary: Stomach ulcers were treated as a degenerative, non-communicable disease of old age, like cholesterol. The only advice was bland food and avoiding stress, and people died horrible deaths. In Australia, Barry Marshall argued it was a simple infectious disease, and nobody believed him. To satisfy Koch's postulates he experimented on himself. He scoped his own healthy stomach, drank water containing Helicobacter pylori, and scoped again to show full-blown ulcers. He then took a simple course of antibiotics and scoped a third time to show they were gone. He won the 2005 Nobel Prize for Medicine.
stories.insight: When a whole field has put a problem in the wrong category, incremental work inside that frame can't help. Sometimes one heretic has to become the experiment.
stories.quote: So he sort of deliberately took the bacteria into his own body and went through the course of antibiotics and it got cleared up.

stories.topic: Charles Dotter borrows a salesman's blowtorch
stories.summary: Charles Dotter pioneered angioplasty in other parts of the body from the 1960s. He was openly rebellious and a lifelong tinkerer who reasoned from first principles that the heart is ultimately a physical object. His favourite 'conceptual trademark' was a sketch of a crossed pipe and wrench, and he assembled catheters in his own kitchen. At an early-1960s conference, travelling salesman Bill Cook noticed a short, bald man with darting eyes sitting on a box behind his stall, which made him nervous. At closing time the stranger asked to borrow his blowtorch and some Teflon tubing to practise making catheters in his hotel room. Cook thought he had 'a real space cadet' on his hands, but agreed. Next morning Dotter returned with ten beautifully made catheters, which Cook sold that day for ten dollars each. Cook called him his 'first production employee', and went on to found the company that led the angioplasty-equipment market.
stories.insight: Dotter was a thinker, not just a technician. He questioned the principles and then built the thing with his own hands.
stories.quote: The next morning he was waiting for me with ten beautifully made Teflon catheters and my blowtorch.

stories.topic: Andreas Gruentzig and the first coronary angioplasty (1977)
stories.summary: Andreas Gruentzig was much younger than Dotter and thought the same way, but had the opposite temperament: he played the system. Bypass surgery had been common since the 1960s, and he asked why the chest needed to be opened when a catheter could carry a balloon to the blockage. Textbooks and top surgeons said it would trigger ventricular fibrillation and kill patients within minutes. In 1977 he did it anyway, on around six patients, and when he presented the results he got a standing ovation. Early on, 30–40% of patients still needed a bypass, but they would have needed one anyway. Stent pioneers then faced the same resistance, because a stent can't be removed from the heart once it's in. Stents arrived in the 1980s and were routine by the mid-1990s. In 2025 Amit was conscious through the whole procedure and was told he now had the heart of a twenty-year-old.
stories.insight: Each stage, first the balloon and then the stent, had to defeat conventional wisdom all over again. It took both the outsider who says 'fuck you' and the insider who persuades.
stories.quote: Gruentzig is a guy who knows that you gotta play the system, that you gotta write the papers in the right order, that you've got to convince the people, you gotta be polite to everyone.

stories.summary: Suggested to Amit by Pranay Kotasthane. The conventional ODI template was that openers build, the middle order consolidates, and everyone slogs in the last ten overs. Mark Greatbatch had hit early in 1992, but it didn't catch on; India tried Kapil Dev as an opener for one match and gave up. Underdog Sri Lanka, much like India in 1983, reasoned that they were weaker in every other department and needed a tactical edge. Since field restrictions made boundaries more profitable early, they promoted two lower-order batsmen, Romesh Kaluwitharana and Sanath Jayasuriya, to open and attack from ball one. The shock and awe worked, and with Muralitharan and a young Chaminda Vaas also in the side, they won the World Cup.
stories.insight: When you're outgunned, strategy derived from the rules can beat talent. Underdogs also have the least to lose from heresy.
stories.quote: So we will put two of our otherwise considered lower order batsmen at the time, we will put them up the order, we will ask them to open the innings and we will ask them to go bang bang bang from the start.

stories.topic: Always bet on the team batting second
stories.summary: Around 2016, a poker friend who bet on cricket asked Amit for an IPL strategy. Amit had played professional poker from 2010 to 2015 but doesn't bet on cricket himself. His advice was to wait for the toss and always back the team batting second. After fourteen games, thirteen had been won by the chasing side. Knowing the target should give at most a 55-45 or 60-40 edge. The real cause was that teams batting first underestimated the par score and didn't go hard enough. That season RCB lost four in a row batting first, and captain Virat Kohli said the batsmen had done their job and the bowlers couldn't defend. Amit found that excuse pathetic: the batsmen had followed the wrong brief.
stories.insight: When a whole league shares the same wrong conventional wisdom, the error shows up as a systematic, exploitable edge.
stories.quote: Because every team would underestimate the par score while batting first and not go hard enough, and then they would lose.

stories.topic: Netflix disrupts Blockbuster, then disrupts itself
stories.summary: In the late 1990s Blockbuster dominated American home video. You had to visit a store with a limited collection, and pay late fees if you didn't return the rental on time. From 1997 Netflix mailed DVDs with no late fees, soon on a monthly subscription, with a near-unlimited catalogue browsable on the web. Blockbuster dismissed it as a niche until Netflix had 4.2 million subscribers by 2004, and copied it too late. In 2007, when internet speeds and screens made streaming seem absurd, Netflix moved into streaming anyway, reasoning that someone else would otherwise kill their business. Five or six years later came original shows like House of Cards and Orange Is the New Black, dropped a whole season at once against the appointment-viewing model, and binge-watching became the norm.
stories.insight: Kodak saw digital photography coming but protected its market. BlackBerry was sure people wanted physical keyboards, and Nokia was disrupted too. Netflix kept attacking its own business before anyone else could. Amit, who often criticises Netflix's conduct in India, credits it fully for this.
stories.quote: If we don't do it, somebody else will, and our business will get over.

stories.topic: Govind Nihalani's missing copy of Party
stories.summary: Around 2010, director Govind Nihalani wanted to film Amit's 2009 novel. Amit naively tried to talk him out of it, then helped write a treatment. Despite Nihalani having made Ardh Satya and Tamas, nobody would fund it. Nihalani suggested the Marathi industry, which he said was like Hindi cinema of the 1980s for independent film, so Amit wrote a Pune-based treatment. Then he lost touch and was too embarrassed to reconnect, and the film was never made. Nihalani once told him his one regret was not having a copy of his own iconic film Party, which wasn't available in India. Amit's New York friend Ved Sharma found it on Netflix, rented it, paid the lost-disc charge, and mailed the DVD. By then Amit had lost touch and inertia had set in, so it never reached Nihalani. Amit believes he got a copy from elsewhere.
stories.insight: Even a great director couldn't get an independent film funded. Netflix's 'unlimited catalogue' held a film its own maker couldn't find in his own country.
stories.quote: But I remember he told me Amit I have one regret, I don't have a copy of Party.

stories.topic: Sonictown: iTunes and MySpace from Bombay, in 2000
stories.summary: In 1999, in his early twenties, Amit was shown the godown of Magnasound, Shashi Gopal's label behind Daler Mehndi, Alisha Chinai and Baba Sehgal. Thousands of CDs from foreign collaborators sat there, and Gopal told him to take what he wanted. Amit told him that in ten years they would all be worthless, because all music would be digital and sold online. He convinced Gopal and marketing head Sunil Mengrajani, and the three became equal partners in Sonictown, which got a double spread in Business World. This was the Napster era, when labels wanted to crush digital. Even so, Sunil secured rights to 80,000 tracks from US labels. In a New York room of investors in early 2000, Amit pitched online song sales plus pages where musicians could connect with each other and update fans. The room was excited, and then the Nasdaq crashed. A second venture later left him deeply in debt.
stories.insight: Being early is indistinguishable from being wrong. Amit says he had the wrong time and the wrong place (Bombay, not Silicon Valley or New York). Many others probably had the same idea, which is survivorship bias in action. The answer is persistence and a bias for action, not giving up on bold ideas.
stories.quote: I laid out what was basically MySpace and I laid out what was basically iTunes.

core_ideas.concept: Incumbents optimize; disruptors rethink the fundamentals
core_ideas.explanation: Taken from Morgan Brown's line on DeepSeek. Conventional players polish the existing process, while progress comes from those who ask whether the whole approach is wrong, and who are usually maligned as heretics for it. Amit makes this the episode's spine, across medicine, cricket and business.
core_ideas.quote: And indeed the only thing that leads to human progress is rethinking the fundamentals. There's absolutely nothing else.

core_ideas.explanation: From Paul Graham's Four Quadrants of Conformism. The real enemies of progress aren't merely conventional people, but those who defend convention aggressively, because a challenge to it feels like an attack on their worldview. Sauerbruch's sneer at Forssmann is the archetype.
core_ideas.quote: They will get in the way of all progress because a challenge to their conventional thinking almost feels like a personal affront because it is challenging their worldview.

core_ideas.explanation: A distinction Ajay once made, which Amit applies to medicine. Technicians master trained procedures and can be superb surgeons. Thinkers like Charles Dotter step back, go to first principles ('the heart is a physical object'; what a plumber does to pipes can be done to blood vessels) and question how things are done. The best do both.
core_ideas.quote: A technician has been trained how to do particular procedures and they might be very skilled and you will have skilled surgeons who are good technicians and nothing else. But our man here, Charles Dotter, is a thinker.

core_ideas.concept: Strategy lags rule changes by years or decades
core_ideas.explanation: When a game's format changes, the optimal strategy changes too, but players keep the old rhythm. Gavaskar batted through a 60-over match for 36 not out in 1975 as if it were Test cricket. Sri Lanka's 1996 heresy and England's later ODI revolution came decades after one-day cricket began. Even after a heretic is proven right, adoption is slow.
core_ideas.quote: every time there is a disruptive change in form, which demands a change in strategy. That change in strategy takes a lag of years or even decades.

core_ideas.concept: The expected value of aggression in T20
core_ideas.explanation: Think like an economist about scarce resources. With the same eleven batsmen but only twenty overs, each dot ball costs more and each wicket costs less. So you front-load: send hitters early, keep hitting whatever falls, and hold the anchor back for emergencies. West Indies won a T20 World Cup doing this, and England applied the logic back to ODIs, making 300-plus scores common worldwide.
core_ideas.quote: This increases the cost of a dot ball, a ball of which you score nothing, and it decreases the cost of a wicket because you have more wickets per over. And therefore the logical conclusion is that the expected value, the EV of aggression goes up.

core_ideas.concept: A slow scorer's runs can be a liability
core_ideas.explanation: In T20, runs alone mislead; what matters is scoring rate relative to the par score. A batsman scoring below the par rate burdens his teammates in proportion to how long he bats. So a 900-run season at a sub-par rate isn't a triumph.
core_ideas.quote: he's a liability to the exact extent of the runs he's made. If he's made more runs, he's more of a liability.

core_ideas.concept: Disrupt yourself before someone else does
core_ideas.explanation: Kodak saw digital photography coming but protected its film business. BlackBerry assumed people wanted physical keyboards, and Nokia was disrupted too. Netflix kept cannibalising itself: mail-order DVDs to streaming before the technology was ready, then original content and whole-season drops. Incumbents fail because the safe move inside a big company is to protect the present.
core_ideas.quote: But internally a big company is always doing the safe thing and protecting its market. And why would I disrupt myself?

core_ideas.concept: Outside-the-box thinking is necessary but not sufficient
core_ideas.explanation: Amit's Sonictown pitch was essentially iTunes and MySpace, years early, from Bombay. Right ideas fail at the wrong time and place, and many others likely had the same idea. The answer isn't to stop trying but to persist and keep throwing things at the world so luck has more chances to find you.
core_ideas.quote: Thinking outside the box is a necessary but not sufficient condition. You also need luck, but you also need persistence because that is how you increase your surface area of serendipity.

core_ideas.concept: Disruption needs a culture of irreverence
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay's first pillar. Societies that regiment children, push them into competitive exams and punish deviation produce conformists, and their talent ends up as bankers. A more easygoing culture tolerates heretics, dropouts and failures; most will go nowhere, but a few become remarkable. Amit adds that Silicon Valley works partly because the culture makes it okay to fail and to be a maverick.
core_ideas.quote: So more stifling societies just make stultified people and we are less likely to get thinking from them.

core_ideas.explanation: Ajay argues there was no path to Unix except through the American counterculture. That cultural difference helps answer the great question of the twentieth century: why the Soviet Union never got to computers, CPUs, Unix and the internet. Amit notes, in passing, that China's DeepSeek is open source while OpenAI and Gemini are not.
core_ideas.quote: There's a direct line from the hippie culture to Unix. There's no way to get to UNIX without the hippie culture.

core_ideas.concept: Gatekeepers decide whether a society progresses
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay's second pillar. The 'commanding heights' of a society are held by allocators: venture capitalists, research funders, journal editors, patent offices and licensing bureaucracies. In India, all too often, everything is banned unless explicitly permitted. If allocators reward conformity, researchers stop thinking and just 'polish the apple'. Shruti Rajagopalan's Emergent Ventures India is the counter-model.
core_ideas.quote: My experience has been that my best papers get rejected. It's just when I am incremental, I play within the game that has been defined, I offer incremental innovation, that is what the journals will accept.

core_ideas.concept: Embrace survivorship bias: honour failure, don't worship winners
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay's third pillar. Success is drawn from a large pool of risk-takers, many of whose lives get chewed up, as with Amit's Nasdaq-crashed startup and his debt-laden second venture. You throw a hundred darts and two work out. Marwari-Gujarati business culture and startup culture get this; much of Indian society doesn't.
core_ideas.quote: It doesn't mean that the two are geniuses and the ninety-eight are fools. It just means randomness.

core_ideas.concept: Disruptors are often not nice people
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay's fourth pillar. Maverick dissidents come as a package with their rough edges. Solzhenitsyn, up close, was not a good human being, and the only way to be a dissident in the Soviet Union was to be a weirdo. Newton's writings would look cringeworthy on social media. Modern polite conformity, amplified by social media, is harmful, and we should support 'the nutcases amongst us'. Ajay's own counterpoint: he keeps everyday life orderly and habitual so his brain is saved for creative work.
core_ideas.quote: A lot of the truly cool people, a lot of the truly disruptive people are not nice guys. It just is.

core_ideas.concept: Expanding the Overton window of the possible
core_ideas.explanation: Amit offers Elon Musk as a repeat disruptor, not a survivorship-bias fluke. Musk made electric cars objects of lust, rethought their interface, vertical integration and direct sales, and challenged thinking on reusable rockets and private spaceflight. Even a wild goal like Mars matters, because it widens what people believe can be attempted.
core_ideas.quote: The point is that you're expanding the boundaries of thought. You're expanding the Overton window of what is possible.

core_ideas.concept: To an LLM, a novel discovery looks like an error
core_ideas.explanation: Dwarkesh Patel asked why LLMs, with all human knowledge memorised, haven't made a single new connection that led to a discovery. Michael's answer: anything outside the training data resembles a hallucination. Amit sees some truth in it, but thinks AI isn't only LLMs and will eventually discover things. The enduring human edge is diving into the new without assuming that what hasn't been said must be crap.
core_ideas.quote: To an LLM, a novel discovery is indistinguishable from an error.

core_ideas.concept: Ajay's law: if an LLM can write it, it's not worth writing
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay uses LLMs as a novelty test. If a one-paragraph prompt yields the full paper, the paper is trivial and you should publish the prompt instead. Amit pushes back: by Sturgeon's law most training data is mediocre, so first-pass output will be too, but with careful prompting LLMs are mind-blowing research and learning tools. At most the test should apply to what an LLM can do at the first pass.
core_ideas.quote: If you can supply a prompt and the LLM can write the paper, then you should just publish it as the prompt. Why bother writing the paper?

jokes_and_cultural_references.content: Ajay introduces the show as a dialectic between 'the irresistible force, Amit Varma' and 'the immovable object, me, the time traveller'. Amit replies that it's an apt metaphor, 'because I have felt like a movable object recently. But thankfully I haven't been moved.'

Why the full-sleeve shirt? Amit says he got feedback he was showing too much skin: 'I didn't want virality to be achieved by raw sex appeal, but by the power of our ideas.' The real reason is that half his arm is shaved from the procedure.
Lancelot Pinto's verdict on Amit's lungs: 'These might even be the best lungs in South Asia, Ajay Shah. Not his words, mine.'

Having been desensitized to aspirin, Amit notes that Ajay is 'allergic to communists. But that matter can be solved. Some communists can be good people'. Ajay proposes a 'communism desensitization program', and Amit signs him up for it, 'though it won't work on me.'

Sudhir Sarnobat called Ajay to say the procedure went well and reported back that Ajay is 'an extremely expressionless man. I said I'm Sudhir speaking and he just said okay.' Amit had imagined Ajay seeing Sudhir's name flash on the caller ID and concluding Amit was dead.

Riffing on Ajay's point about silent snake bites, Amit imagines the Shah–Thomas bedroom at night: Ajay wakes and asks, 'Susan, did you bite me just now?', she tells him to fuck off and goes back to sleep, 'at which point you realize the horrible truth.'

Amit on his hospital bill: 'this can be a perpetual heart attack machine'. You have a heart attack, get the procedure, see the bill, have another heart attack, and so on, with the game-theoretic catch that the surgeon must keep you alive long enough to pay the next bill. Ajay diagnoses 'Zeno-phobia', 'the irrational fear of convergent sequences', after Zeno's paradox. Amit: 'This is the finest analysis of a bad joke I have ever seen. Sashtang pranam.'

When Ajay credits the thousands of innovations that brought medicine to 'the state of healing Amit Varma', Amit replies: 'All the amazing people that brought me here in front of you are really my parents and their parents before them and so on down the line all the way to a woman in Africa and even she had parents.'
Contrasting the two angioplasty pioneers: Dotter 'is happy to say fuck you to everyone, kinda like me', while Gruentzig knows 'you gotta be polite to everyone. Kinda like you.'
On Gukesh's heart rate of 62 in a crucial position: 'Sixty two, like I don't even have sixty two when I'm doing nothing.'

Blockbuster's late fees were 'punishing the Bengali procrastinator, which is not a good thing'. When Amit admits the Netflix DVD of Party never reached Nihalani, Ajay worries that 'DVDs became obsolete and there were no DVD players left in the world' in the time Amit took.
Ajay on cultural permissiveness: 'Very many people will go off to the beaches of Goa and get doped out, but a small fraction of them will become amazing people.'

After Ajay says disruptors require 'being a little less Amit Varma', Amit notes he has been implied to be 'A, not a nice guy, B a weirdo, and C one of the nut cases among us'. He accepts all of it, and observes that Ajay has agreed with everything this episode because 'poor guy, his heart. I just won't mess with it.'

Praising Emergent Ventures: conventional allocators are 'missing the freaks, we are missing the nutcases, we are missing the Amit Varmas.' Amit closes the AI argument on theme: 'And you are restating fundamental thinking. I am challenging them, Ajay Shah.'

Ferdinand Sauerbruch's dismissal of Forssmann, Amit's emblem of the aggressively conventional minded: 'With such experiments you might habilitate in a circus, but these have no place in a decent German hospital.'

Amit describes his own angioplasty as a video game: three screens beside him like a day trader's setup, a doctor with what is practically a game controller, and, 'like in a game of Pac-Man', manoeuvring through the arteries zapping clots.

Ajay quotes a friend's pithy line, 'the heart is a solved problem'. Amit's answer: biologically yes ('cardiac is solved, cancer is the next target'), 'but metaphorically the heart is, no one can solve the heart.'
Sunil Gavaskar's 36 not out in a 60-over match at the 1975 World Cup: Amit's example of players carrying Test-match rhythms into a new format whose incentives had changed.

Chess heart-rate tracking: Amit watched Sindarov's heart rate hit 150–155 against Nakamura's 126–127 in their tie-breaks. Peter Leko, seeing Gukesh at 62 in a crucial position, said that now he knew why Gukesh is world champion.
Sturgeon's law, '95 percent of everything is crap', which Amit uses to explain why default LLM writing is mediocre: the data it learns from mostly is.
Magnasound, the label behind Daler Mehndi, Alisha Chinai and Baba Sehgal, set against the Napster era, when labels wanted to crush digital music rather than embrace it.
